 The College of Fisheries and Ocean Sciences at University of Alaska Fairbanks (UAF) and Dr. Andy Seitz research lab, invites individuals to submit a statement of interest for the position of Fisheries Technician on our hydrokinetic energy research team. Please note, this is not the formal application process but an initial step to express interest. This position is part of a study assessing the impacts of hydrokinetic turbines on fish populations in the Yukon River in Interior Alaska. The successful candidate will work as a seasonal technician in spring and summer 2027 and, upon acceptance into the graduate program at UAF, transition into a funded Master of Science program in Fisheries at UAF beginning Fall 2027.

The primary responsibilities of this position include: 1) conducting baseline research to describe the fish community in the Yukon River near the village of Galena, AK; 2) monitoring lateral distribution of down-migrating salmon using fyke nets and an inclined plane trap; 3) modeling the probability of salmon collisions with hydrokinetic energy devices; and 4) working with local stakeholders to describe community perceptions of fisheries interactions with turbines.

UAF is committed to building a culturally diverse and inclusive organization. I am recruiting one or more MS or PhD students to join my lab in the Department of Biology at the
University of North Dakota, with a target start of Summer/Fall 2027. This is a new lab so incoming
students will have real input into shaping its culture and research direction.

My research examines food web and trophic dynamics in freshwater ecosystems using diet, stable isotope
and other approaches, with particular interest in how climate change and disturbance (wildfire, shifting
thermal and hydrologic regimes) reshape lake and stream food webs. My own field experience spans
watersheds in Alaska and the Pacific Northwest, but I'm equally interested in students who want to

directions include, but are not limited to:
●Fish and invertebrate secondary production in streams, rivers, and lakes
●Trophic responses of lakes and streams to wildfire or other acute disturbances
●Climate-driven shifts in thermal regime and cascading effects on food webs
●Braided river channel production and food web dynamics
●Stable isotope and biomarker approaches to tracking energy flow in aquatic systems
●Comparative food web structure across gradients of hydrologic connectivity or land use

Students will be trained in traditional stream ecology, stable isotope methods, quantitative food web
analysis, field sampling design, statistical/programming approaches (R), and scientific writing, and will
be supported in attending and presenting at national conferences.

Dr. Alison O’Dowd (https://www.humboldt.edu/environmental-science-and-management/alison-odowd) at Cal Poly Humboldt seeks applications for highly motivated students interested in pursuing graduate school in the Environmental Science & Management option of the Natural Resources Graduate Program (https://www.humboldt.edu/cnrs/graduate-programs/natural-resources). Students with an interest in estuarine invertebrates, aquatic food webs, bioenergetics models, and invertebrates as food resources for juvenile salmonids are particularly encouraged to apply.

Project Summary
The objective of this research is to understand the impact of a restoration project in the Eel River Estuary (at Cannibal Island in Northern California) on rearing habitat and landscape-scale growth potential for juvenile salmonids and other native fish species that inhabit the site. To do this, we will quantify the changes in rearing habitat (i.e., area, water quality characteristics, and invertebrate biomass availability) and potential bioenergetic differences (derived from observed differences in invertebrate biomass) for juvenile salmonids (Chinook, Coho) and other fish in the assemblage. The proposed approach is to collect pre- and post- restoration food web, water quality, and physical habitat data, stage and velocity at monthly intervals, in the restoration area and a nearby control site, during periods of key estuary rearing for juvenile salmonids (e.g. December-August). These data can be evaluated as meaningful stand-alone metrics (e.g. changes in invertebrate density and biomass, water quality and physical habitat) and integrated into a bioenergetics model to predict changes on landscape scale productivity (e.g. joules of fish growth potential per area per time). We will also explore the role of Cannibal Island as a producer and exporter of food to adjacent foraging habitat in the North Bay of the Eel River Estuary pre- and post-restoration construction. 

This graduate research project will seek to understand the invertebrate responses post-restoration to assess food resources for out-migrating juvenile salmonids and other fish. Collection and identification of estuarine invertebrates, building a bioenergetics model, and interpretation of data will be the primary tasks associated with this project.

-          Demonstrated experience managing others in a laboratory setting

Description
With support from Montana Fish, Wildlife, and Parks, the University of Montana Fish and Wildlife Genomics Lab is recruiting a PhD student that will focus their efforts on several outstanding questions concerning hybridization between native cutthroat trout and introduced rainbow trout.  Conservation geneticists and fisheries managers in the state of Montana have been focused on describing, monitoring, understanding, and addressing hybridization between native cutthroat trout and rainbow trout for 50 years. Indeed, rainbow trout hybridization is often considered the primary threat to native cutthroat trout in Montana (and beyond).  However, long-term and spatially extensive data collections are beginning to reveal widely varying patterns of hybridization across space, and divergent changes in hybridization through time.  This project will use multiple sources of information to modernize our understanding of the threat of non-native hybridization for cutthroat trout conservation.  The ultimate goal of this project is to leverage various existing resources, including what is likely the world’s most extensive hybridization monitoring program, to better identify what management strategies will be most appropriate for cutthroat trout across Montana.    

This project includes two collaborative parts: (1) a post-doctoral student will focus on potential genomic mechanisms (e.g., incompatibilities) that may explain observed differences in hybridization across the state; and (2) the PhD project being advertised here will use long-term, spatially extensive data to better describe hybridization dynamics, and the potential factors that may explain heterogenous hybridization outcomes.  There are nearly 50 years of genetic data describing the extent of rainbow trout hybridization in cutthroat trout populations in Montana, including more than 100,000 individually genotyped fish.  These foundational monitoring data provide a remarkable opportunity to better describe both spatial and temporal patterns of hybridization across all cold-water habitats in the state over decades.  Specific research questions include (but are not limited to):

1.     How has the extent of rainbow trout hybridization changed across different watersheds in Montana?  

2.     Do spatial and temporal changes (increases) in rainbow trout hybridization match expectations based on abundance and distribution of rainbow trout, environmental conditions, or random mating?

3.     How common is genomic extinction, and what landscape features (e.g., isolation vs. connectivity) are associated with genomic extinction across space and time?

4.     Can spatial and temporal changes in hybridization be explained by genomic incompatibilities described/identified with genomic results? (in collaboration with post-doc)

Ultimately, these questions (and other related questions) will be used, along with genomic analyses above, to better identify the mechanisms that promote or resist rainbow trout hybridization across WCT and YCT populations in Montana.  Overall, this work will be used to directly identify those geographic regions (or environmental or genomic conditions) that are most susceptible and to rainbow trout hybridization, and in contrast, those that appear most resilient.  In so doing, this project will help biologists and managers more accurately assess risk across the wide variety of environmental conditions and intrinsic genetic/genomic variability found in cutthroat trout, both within and between species.  While the project clearly has a defined conservation focus, the overall topic and the unprecedented data set leaves opportunity to directly address key questions in the broader fields of population genetics and evolutionary ecology.

The ideal candidate for this position will have a solid understanding of population genetics, but equally importantly, experience with (or strong desire to learn) modern statistical approaches to data analysis (e.g., generalized mixed modeling, Bayesian modeling, etc.), and data generation (e.g., environmental data).  Preferred skills include strong bioinformatic skills, programming in R or Python, and strong communication skills.

Available funding provides 4-years of PhD support (6 semesters of RA support, 2 semesters of TA support).  Student would be located at the University of Montana and be a part of the Wildlife Biology Program.  

Anticipated start date January 1, 2027. The prospective student would need to apply to the UM Graduate School by November 15, 2026. Application review will begin October 15th.

The Department of Forestry in the College of Forest Resources and the Forest and Wildlife Research Center at Mississippi State University is seeking applicants for a funded M.S. assistantship to examine the professional readiness of forestry graduates and the competency needs of employers across public, private, and non-profit natural resource sectors. The student will be advised by Dr. Arun Regmi and will join the social dimensions research program in the Department of Forestry.
 
This research will investigate how existing educational experiences prepare students for careers in the field and evaluate employer expectations for entry-level professionals. By engaging recent graduates, employers, and other stakeholders, the project will identify areas of alignment and potential gaps between educational preparation and professional competency needs. The student will contribute to all aspects of the research, including survey and protocol development, data collection, stakeholder engagement, qualitative and quantitative analysis, scientific writing, and dissemination of findings. The successful candidate will be self-motivated, creative, and eager to collaborate in a multidisciplinary environment.

Description
The Wisely Lab in the University of Florida Department of Wildlife Ecology and Conservation is recruiting a Ph.D. student to join a multidisciplinary project developing innovative approaches for surveillance of feral swine and African swine fever virus (ASFV).

The project uses mosquito bloodmeals as biological samples of free-ranging feral swine, an approach known as exogenous xenosurveillance. By treating blood-fed mosquitoes as “flying syringes,” the research team will evaluate whether mosquito bloodmeals can be used to detect feral swine, genetically identify individual animals, estimate population abundance, and support pathogen surveillance.


Position responsibilities

The Ph.D. student will take a leading role in the field ecology and quantitative components of the project. Responsibilities will include:

·         Coordinating deployment and sampling of camera traps and mosquito capture systems across wet and dry seasons.

·         Supervising and mentoring undergraduate researchers participating in field and laboratory activities.

·         Working with project collaborators to process mosquito bloodmeals and generate genetic data for individual identification of feral swine.

·         Developing genetic mark-recapture models to estimate feral swine abundance from mosquito-derived host DNA.

·         AND/OR

·         Developing occupancy/detection models to compare the effectiveness of mosquito-based surveillance and conventional camera trapping.

The student will be co-advised by Dr. Samantha Wisely, a wildlife disease ecologist in UF's Department of Wildlife Ecology and Conservation, and Dr. Nathan Burkett-Cadena, a vector-borne disease ecologist at the UF Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory. The student will also collaborate closely with Dr. Tim Smyser of the USDA APHIS Wildlife Services National Feral Swine Damage Management Program on genomic approaches for individual identification of feral swine. The student will have the opportunity to also interact with Dr. Amy Vittor from the College of Medicine on serological assay development. 

An important feature of the project is the integration of research with agricultural biosecurity education. The successful candidate will work closely with a Ph.D. student specializing in science communication/agricultural education, sharing field experiences, data and scientific expertise that will inform educational materials, microcredentials and a graduate learning module in genetic mark-recapture. The science communications Ph.D. student, mentored by Dr. Grady Roberts, will lead development of the educational products; this position will contribute scientific content and collaborate on their development but will not lead the project's education component.


Minimum qualifications

Applicants should have:

·         A bachelor's or master's degree in wildlife ecology, ecology, entomology, biology, quantitative ecology, disease ecology, or a related field.

·         Previous experience conducting ecological field research.

·         Demonstrated interest in wildlife population ecology, wildlife disease, quantitative ecology, or wildlife surveillance.

·         Experience with, or strong interest in learning, population modeling and statistical analysis in R.

·         Ability and willingness to conduct extended fieldwork under hot, humid and physically demanding Florida conditions.

·         Strong organizational, written communication and teamwork skills.

·         Ability to work independently while contributing effectively to a highly interdisciplinary research team.

Experience with camera trapping, mosquito or other arthropod sampling, molecular ecology/genetics, occupancy modeling, capture-recapture analysis, or supervision of field crews is desirable but not required.


Research environment

The student will join a collaborative team spanning wildlife disease ecology, entomology, genomics, infectious disease and agricultural education, with collaborators at the University of Florida and USDA APHIS Wildlife Services. The project provides an unusual opportunity for a doctoral student to integrate intensive field ecology with molecular tools and quantitative population modeling while conducting research with direct application to wildlife management and U.S. agricultural biosecurity. 

Location: University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, with substantial fieldwork throughout Florida.
Degree: Ph.D. in Wildlife Ecology and Conservation
Advisor: Wisely, with co-advising by Nathan Burkett-Cadena

This USDA AFRI funded graduate assistanceship has four years of funding and would begin in May of 2027. Please send a cv and cover letter to Samantha Wisely at [email removed] by November 15, 2026.

We are recruiting one Ph.D. student or one MS student to conduct research which broadly aims to assess the space use and resource selection of White-winged Doves (Zenaida asiatica) in South Texas in the non-breeding season to expand on work currently being conducted in the Smith Lab at The Caesar Kleberg Wildlife Research Institute, Texas A&M-Kingsville.     Description
 The Avian Ecology Program at Archbold Biological Station is seeking four Post-Baccalaureate Research Fellows (PBRFs) for seasonal appointments of at least six months to assist with one of the world's longest-running studies of wild birds: a 57-year research program focused on the demography, ecology, behavior, and conservation of the federally threatened Florida Scrub-Jay (Aphelocoma coerulescens). Four positions will begin on February 1, 2027. Two appointments will continue through July 2027, while the remaining two will continue through mid-September 2027. 

 Fellows will be mentored by Dr. Sahas Barve and work within a dynamic research team that includes three research assistants. This is a seasonal position paying $15.00 per hour for approximately 29 hours per week. Because this position is classified as seasonal, traditional employee benefits are not provided at hire. Archbold determines benefit eligibility for seasonal employees using the Affordable Care Act (ACA) look-back measurement method. 

 Lodging is provided, and residence at Archbold Biological Station is required for the duration of the fellowship. 

 A unique feature of this fellowship is the opportunity to develop an independent research project, either through the collection of new field data or by leveraging Archbold's extensive long-term Florida Scrub-Jay dataset. We particularly encourage applications from individuals who are enthusiastic about pursuing independent research and gaining hands-on experience in ecological field studies, data analysis, and scientific inquiry. 

 
Requirements
Key Responsibilities 
 PBRFs contribute to several aspects of this research, but their primary duties include:  
 Independently searching for and monitoring nests  
 Conducting monthly censuses of color-banded birds 
 Daily data entry 
 Habituating birds for subsequent trapping 
 Conducting oak acorn surveys  
 Surveying FLSJ populations at other sites 
 In addition, PBRFs may assist in collecting blood samples from jays, mapping jay territories, and helping with prescribed fires  

Required Qualifications 
 Bachelor’s degree. This position is ideal for students with undergraduate degrees contemplating graduate school in the fields of Ecology, Evolution, Conservation Biology, and Natural Resource Management.  


 Experience
 Field experience outside of coursework; however, we provide all required training for all PBRFs.  
 Resighting color-banded birds 
 Finding and monitoring nests 
 Using a compass or GPS  
 Ability to navigate and work alone in the field but coordinate duties with a small team to achieve all project goals. 
 Certifications/Licenses 
 A valid US Driver’s License  
 Experience searching for nests of open-cup nesters, preferred 
 Please note that we are unable to provide international applicants with a work visa. US citizenship or permission to work legally in the US is required.


 Knowledge, Skills, and Abilities
 Attention to detail with respect to following sampling protocols and managing data 
 Tolerance for biting insects, early mornings, and high heat/humidity 
 Motivation and enthusiasm about living and working at a rural field-station 
 Respect for others, as PBRFs will share lodging with other PBRFs 
 Effective and responsive communication with supervisors, coworkers, and roommates 

 
Work Environment & Physical Requirements
 Employees must be able to perform the essential functions of their position with or without reasonable accommodation. Depending on the role, work may require sitting, standing, walking, bending, reaching, lifting and carrying materials, repetitive hand movements, and operating standard office, laboratory, field, or maintenance equipment. Some positions may involve working outdoors in varying weather conditions, traversing uneven terrain, and occasional travel. Physical requirements will vary by position and will be specified in the individual job description. 
   

 Why Join Archbold?
 Joining Archbold means becoming part of a mission-driven organization dedicated to advancing scientific research, conservation, and education. Employees have the opportunity to contribute meaningful work that supports the understanding and preservation of natural ecosystems while collaborating with passionate, talented professionals. Archbold fosters a culture of innovation, teamwork, and continuous learning, providing an environment where employees can grow professionally while making a lasting impact on science, conservation, and the communities we serve. Eligible employees also enjoy competitive compensation and benefits package designed to support their well-being and professional success.

 Complete the application here, and include the following in a single pdf titled with your surname: 
 A single-page cover letter outlining how your previous experiences and interests are relevant to the job responsibilities and qualifications listed above. Be sure to mention your research interests and describe how this position aligns with your personal experiences and goals. 
A CV
The names and contact information of three references 


For questions, please contact Hannah Miller ([email removed]). We will start reviewing applications after the deadline on October 20, 2026, and hope to finalize hires by ~1 month after this date.

Description
The New Mexico Highlands University Department of Forestry invites applicants to fill one or more nine-month, tenure-track faculty positions beginning as early as August 2027.

The successful candidates will be responsible for teaching a range of forestry and natural resources management courses per academic year; conducting research and scholarship that engages both undergraduate and graduate students; serving the University, professional organizations, and the broader community of natural resources stakeholders; advising Forestry Department students; contributing to the modernization and improvement of the Forestry and Conservation Management curricula; participating in the Forestry Department’s outcomes assessments, aiding in the maintenance of Society of American Foresters (SAF) accreditation, and establishing and maintaining relationships with industry, tribal, governmental, and non-governmental partners. Preferred areas of specialization include tree ecophysiology, forest ecohydrology, water resources or watershed management.  Regardless of specialty, individuals with proficiency in plant production and forest nursery management, applied forest ecology, and forest management and GIS are strongly encouraged to apply. 

This position is part of the NMHU College of Arts and Sciences’ initiative to strengthen its Forestry Department’s teaching and research capabilities. The College of Arts and Sciences, housed within a Hispanic Serving Institution, is dedicated to creating a climate of engagement, diversity and inclusion, and providing pathways for students from underrepresented groups to pursue STEM careers. All applicants should have a demonstrated willingness to work collaboratively with faculty from a wide range of disciplines, cultures, and academic backgrounds and to advise and teach an undergraduate and graduate student body that is diverse with respect to socio-economic status, culture, and career path.

The successful candidate will be expected to seek and acquire external research support and collaborate with universities, state and federal government agencies, and non-governmental organizations in the areas of specialization. 

The New Mexico Forest and Watershed Restoration Institute, which is housed on NMHU’s main campus, utilizes NMHU faculty members and students in projects throughout the state. NMHU Forestry faculty also regularly collaborate with the faculty and staff of New Mexico State University's (NMSU) John T. Harrington Forestry Research Center in Mora, NM, as well as the New Mexico Reforestation Center, with facilities and operations in both Mora, NM and on NMHU’s Las Vegas campus. Building upon our current strengths, the incumbent will be expected to contribute to the development of a nationally recognized education, research, and outreach program focused on forest or wildland fire management and/or forest or wildland ecosystem health. Preference will be given to candidates with a demonstrated ability or willingness to concentrate on these themes in relation to Southern Rocky Mountains and Southwestern ecosystems. NMHU has strong ties with the USDA Forest Service, USDOI Fish and Wildlife Service, National Park Service, NM Forestry Division, Los Alamos National Laboratory, and other private and non-governmental organizations and is growing its international footprint.

Description
 We are seeking a highly motivated Postdoctoral Associate to join the laboratory of Samantha M. Wisely for a research project investigating the landscape genetics and molecular ecology of Wild Turkeys (Meleagris gallopavo) in Florida. 

The successful candidate will lead genetic and genomic analyses designed to better understand the ecological and evolutionary processes influencing Wild Turkey populations across Florida. The project will integrate molecular data with spatial and ecological information to investigate patterns of genetic connectivity, population structure, dispersal, relatedness, and reproduction across heterogeneous landscapes. 

A major emphasis of the position will be the use of spatial and landscape genetic approaches to determine how environmental and anthropogenic landscape features influence gene flow and population connectivity. The project will also incorporate parentage and relatedness analyses to examine reproductive relationships and fine-scale patterns of movement and population structure. 


Primary Responsibilities 

The successful candidate will be expected to: 

·         Lead analyses of molecular genetic/genomic datasets from Wild Turkey populations throughout Florida. 

·         Conduct population genetic and landscape genetic analyses, including assessment of population structure, genetic differentiation, connectivity, and gene flow. 

·         Integrate genetic data with GIS and spatial environmental datasets to evaluate landscape effects on genetic connectivity and dispersal. 

·         Conduct parentage, kinship, and relatedness analyses to investigate reproductive relationships and fine-scale population processes. 

·         Collaborate with project investigators, graduate students, agency biologists, and other research partners. 

·         Prepare manuscripts for publication in peer-reviewed journals and present findings at professional scientific meetings. 

·         Assist with mentoring graduate and undergraduate students involved in molecular ecology and wildlife research. 

·         Contribute intellectually to the development of additional research questions and proposals emerging from the project. 


Required Qualifications 

Applicants must have: 

·         A Ph.D. in molecular ecology, conservation genetics, landscape genetics, population genetics, wildlife genomics, or a closely related field by the anticipated start date. 

·         Demonstrated experience analyzing population genetic or genomic datasets. 

·         Experience working in R and/or other programming environments used for genetic and ecological analyses. 

·         A demonstrated ability to conduct independent research and manage large or complex datasets. 

·         Excellent written and oral communication skills. 

·         Ability to work effectively as part of a collaborative, multidisciplinary research team. 


Preferred Qualifications 

Preference will be given to candidates with one or more of the following: 

·         Experience conducting landscape genetic analyses of wildlife populations. 

·         Experience integrating molecular data with GIS, remote-sensing, land-cover, or other spatial datasets. 

·         Expertise with SNP, reduced-representation genomic, or other contemporary molecular datasets. 

·         Experience with population assignment, individual identification, genetic estimates of dispersal, or connectivity modeling. 

·         Experience with parentage analysis involving wild populations. 

·         Familiarity with spatially explicit models of gene flow or resistance/connectivity modeling. 

·         Familiarity with reproducible research workflows, version control, or high-performance computing. 


Research Environment 

The successful applicant will join the Wisely Lab at the University of Florida, an interdisciplinary research group working at the interface of wildlife ecology, molecular ecology, conservation genetics, disease ecology, and wildlife management. 


Expected Salary and Commitment 

Salary will be commensurate with qualifications and experience and consistent with University of Florida guidelines for Postdoctoral Associates. This is a term position for one year with the possibility for renewal for a second year. 


Special Instructions to Applicants 

Please submit the following to [email removed] 

1.      Cover letter describing research interests, relevant experience, and qualifications for the position. The cover letter should specifically describe the applicant's experience with population or landscape genetics, spatial analysis, and parentage/relatedness analysis. 

2.      Curriculum vitae. 

3.      Contact information for three professional references. 

4.      One representative peer-reviewed publication that best demonstrates the applicant's relevant research experience. 

Review of applications will begin November 15th  and will continue until the position is filled.

Title- Ballast Water Vessel Inspector
Classification- Marine Transportation and Safety Specialist 3
Job Status- Full-Time / Permanent
WDFW Program- Fish Program – Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) Management
Duty Station- Ridgefield, Washington – Clark County

Learn more about being a member of Team WDFW!


As the Ballast Water Vessel Inspector, you’ll help protect Washington’s waters from aquatic invasive species and support the long-term health of our marine ecosystems.

In this role, you’ll train to conduct onboard inspections of commercial vessels arriving in Washington State to ensure compliance with ballast water management regulations designed to prevent the spread of invasive species. You’ll work in active port environments throughout the Columbia River, Greys Harbor, and South Puget Sound.

This is a great opportunity for someone interested in maritime operations, environmental compliance, vessel inspection, and protecting Washington’s natural resources through hands-on fieldwork and regulatory enforcement.


What to Expect:
Among the varied range of responsibilities held within this role, the Ballast Water Vessel Inspector will,

Vessel Ballast Water Risk Audits:
Assess daily vessel arrivals to identify the highest ballast water risks using vessel compliance history, department protocols, and professional judgement.
Select, board, and inspect at least 5% of all targeted vessel arrivals in assigned region.
Explain state laws and regulations and assist vessel officers and crew in meeting compliance objectives for state ballast water management.
Complete required department inspection forms per protocols.

Compliance Actions:
Assess onboard evidence of ballast water management compliance using vessel records, equipment specifications, and certifications.
Investigate and issue appropriate compliance actions per department protocols for vessel situations including Warnings, Notices of Correction, or recommendations for Notice of Penalty.
Compile evidence to create professional and legally defensible compliance actions.

Coordination, Planning, and Reporting:
Coordinate with the U.S. Coast Guard, Oregon Department of Environmental Quality, and Washington Department of Ecology to support cooperative vessel management and minimize duplication of efforts on concurrent vessel boardings.
Analyze, evaluate, and interpret vessel inspection data.
Support the development and implementation of work plans, regulatory updates, performance measures, management forms, protocols, and procedures. 
Participate in state, regional, and national work groups as assigned.

Monitoring and Research:
Conduct onboard testing of new protocols and equipment as directed.
Analyze ballast water treatment system (BWTS) voyage maintenance records and annual independent laboratory performance test reports to support the development of new regulatory requirements.
Assist senior staff in developing and evaluating enhanced vessel ballast water and biofouling risk assessment protocols.
Develop, evaluate, and interpret protocols, tools, and performance measures used to assess the effectiveness of ballast water management practices.
 

Working Conditions: 

Work Setting, including hazards:
Work is performed in potentially hazardous industrial port environments aboard merchant vessels conducting cargo operations. Board and inspect all types of vessels in a variety of weather conditions and physically access all areas of vessels, including climbing ladders and entering engine/pump rooms, and occasionally, ballast tanks to inspect ballast management activities. Frequently lift and carry a 40-pound gear bag. Handle hazardous biological sample preservation chemicals, such as Formalin and ethanol. This position may involve working in or near water, including tasks that require navigating, negotiating, and performing duties related to water environments.

Schedule:
This position is full-time, working 40 hours per week. The standard work schedule includes the potential for occasional evening or weekend work as needed. Schedules may vary based on business needs, time of year, and/or weather conditions.

Travel Requirements:
Travel between state ports is required and may average approximately 1,500 to 3,000 miles per month.

Tools and Equipment:
Use appropriate safety equipment including flotation devices, hard hats, safety goggles, and steel-toed boots. 

Customer Interactions:
Regular interaction with regulated industry representatives, including situations that may be complex or confrontational. Communication may also involve working with individuals for whom English is a secondary language.
 

Qualifications:

Required Qualifications:

Option 1– All of the following:
A Bachelor of Science or Master's degree involving major study in one of the following:  
Marine Engineering
Nautical Industrial Science
Naval Architecture
A closely related field
*Four (4) years of professional-level experience in vessel design or vessel inspection.

Option 2 – All of the following (experience may be gained concurrently):
A Bachelor of Science or Master’s degree involving major study in one of the following: 
Environmental Planning 
Natural Sciences 
A closely related field
*Four (4) years of professional-level experience in maritime operations, aquatic invasive species management, environmental compliance, or closely related regulatory or scientific work. 
Including at least two (2) years of professional-level experience in vessel design or vessel inspection.

Option 3– All of the following:
A PhD in one of the following: 
Environmental Planning
Marine Engineering
Natural Sciences
Nautical Industrial Science
Naval Architecture 
A closely related field
*Two (2) years of professional-level experience in vessel design or vessel inspection.

*Qualifying experience must include substantial professional-level work in at least two (2) of the knowledge areas listed below, including at least one (1) area from Part A and one (1) area from Part B:

Part A:
Shipping regulatory and management operations.
Vessel operations.
Vessel and port safety requirements.
Vessel ballast water management system operations, testing, and quality control requirements used for regulatory purposes.
Other related commercial vessel inspection duties, such as oil spill prevention and other vessel discharge.

Part B:
Marine and freshwater Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) risks to the state, including ballast water and biofouling pathways and management techniques. 
Working effectively with diverse vessel managers, agents, officers, and crew.
Field research, sampling, monitoring, and testing techniques.
Other related natural resource duties and responsibilities, such as fishery observations and environmental compliance.

Please Note:
Closely related qualifying experience may be substituted for the required education on a year-by-year basis.
A current Maritime License for Marine Officer or Marine Engineer may substitute for the education requirement.

Certifications/Licenses:
Valid driver’s license.

Special Requirements/Conditions of Employment:
This position will be required to undergo a federal background check as part of obtaining a Transportation Worker Identification Credential (TWIC) or similar federal credential.


Preferred Qualifications:
In addition to the required qualifications, our ideal applicant will possess one or more of the following:
Results Orientation and Initiative: Focuses on results and desired outcomes and how best to achieve them. Proactively identifies needs and takes appropriate action.
Decision Making: Ability to make independent decisions in a manner that produces outcomes that are consistent with Agency, Program, and Division policy is essential. Appropriately involves supervisor or others in decision making.
Communication: Demonstrates clear, concise written and verbal communication skills. Keeps supervisors and co-workers informed of need to know items.
Planning: Uses strategic thinking to evaluate proposed actions and timelines against organizational mission and values. Integrates current plans with other plans as needed to achieve the overall mission.
Relationship Building and Collaboration: Develop and maintain effective internal and external partnerships that promote and support the Agency’s mission and goals.

About Texas A&M AgriLife
Texas A&M AgriLife is comprised of the following Texas A&M University System members:
• Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service
• Texas A&M AgriLife Research
• College of Agriculture and Life Sciences at Texas A&M University
• Texas A&M Forest Service
• Texas A&M Veterinary Medical Diagnostic Laboratory

As the nation’s largest most comprehensive agriculture program, Texas A&M AgriLife brings together a college and four state agencies focused on agriculture and life sciences within The Texas A&M University System. With over 5,000 employees and a presence in every county across the state, Texas A&M AgriLife is uniquely positioned to improve lives, environments and the Texas economy through education, research, extension and service.

Click here to learn more about how you can be a part of AgriLife and make a difference in the world!

Position Information:
Texas A&M AgriLife Research seeks an innovative, collaborative, and highly motivated scientist to serve as an Assistant Professor in Precision Ranching. This is a 12-month, 100% research appointment administratively housed at the Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center in San Angelo, Texas, with strong preference for the candidate to be based primarily at the Texas A&M AgriLife Sonora Experiment Station, where the proposed faculty member will engage closely with regional stakeholders to address their needs through research. The successful candidate will hold an affiliation with either the Department of Rangeland, Wildlife & Fisheries Management or the Department of Biological and Agricultural Engineering at Texas A&M University.
The successful candidate will develop a nationally recognized, externally funded research program focused on advancing the productivity, profitability, and sustainability of rangeland systems through the application of precision technologies, data-driven decision support tools, and integrated resource management strategies. The position will foster interdisciplinary collaborations across Texas A&M AgriLife Research, Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service, Texas A&M University, industry partners, and other stakeholder groups.

Texas rangelands comprise approximately 60% of the state's land area and support livestock production, wildlife habitat, water resources, recreation, agritourism, and numerous ecosystem services. This position will address emerging challenges and opportunities through the application of smart sensing technologies, remote monitoring systems, automation, artificial intelligence, and advanced analytics to improve management decisions and resource stewardship across rangeland enterprises.

Responsibilities:
Develop and maintain an externally funded, nationally recognized research program addressing
critical challenges facing Texas rangeland and livestock industries.
Conduct fundamental, applied, and translational research focused on precision ranching
technologies and management systems.
Advance innovative solutions related to:
Rangeland restoration and management.
Livestock production efficiency and resource optimization.
Smart sensing, automation, and digital agriculture technologies.
Wildfire mitigation and invasive species management.
Watershed management and water quality protection.
Integrated multi-enterprise ranching systems, including agritourism.
Publish research findings in high-impact peer-reviewed journals and other relevant outlets.
Mentor graduate students and supervise research personnel.
Secure competitive extramural funding from federal, state, industry, and private sources.
Collaborate with AgriLife Research and Extension faculty, industry stakeholders, government agencies, and nonprofit organizations.
Translate research outcomes into practical applications that support stakeholder adoption and economic impact.
Contribute to intellectual property development, technology transfer, and stakeholder engagement activities.

Administrative Relationships:
Reports to the Center Director, Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center at San Angelo with academic guidance provided by the affiliated department.
Provides direction and supervision for research personnel, support staff, and graduate students associated with the program.

Qualifications:
Required job qualifications:
Ph.D. in Rangeland Science, Biological and Agricultural Engineering, or a closely related discipline by the date of appointment.
Expertise in rangeland production systems and management practices.
Demonstrated experience with precision agriculture technologies, smart sensor systems, remote sensing, data analytics, automation, or related technologies.
Record of publishing original research in peer-reviewed journals.
Strong written, verbal, and interpersonal communication skills.

Preferred job qualifications:
Demonstrated experience with range plant identification and field-based vegetation sampling.
Prior academic, post-doctoral, or professional research experience.
Demonstrated ability to secure competitive external funding.
Experience working with federal agencies or in other multi-agency collaborative settings.
Ability to build collaborative and multidisciplinary research programs.
Ability to communicate and build relationships with regional stakeholders to identify needs to address through research.

Knowledge, Skills, and Abilities:
Knowledge of rangeland production systems and management practices in semi-arid rangelands, including strong plant identification skills and experience with field sampling methods.
Strong project management and organizational skills.
Demonstrated leadership and team-building capabilities.
Ability to manage multiple projects and priorities effectively.
Professional judgment, initiative, and interpersonal effectiveness.
Understanding of the mission and role of the Land-Grant University System.

A minimum of four years of experience is required, inclusive of PhD education.

Location and Facilities:
Texas A&M AgriLife’s San Angelo Research and Extension Center is an off-campus center located in San Angelo, Texas, known for its long history of work on small ruminant ranching, rangelands and wildlife in the West Central Texas region. Scientists at the center conduct research on site and at satellite stations located in Crockett, Edwards, Sutton, and Menard counties, totaling about 15,000 acres. Each location has all the equipment required for managing the livestock on these properties including cross fencing, corrals, livestock scales, barns, and storage facilities.

Sonora Station (Sutton and Edwards counties) recently celebrated its 110th anniversary as a research facility. Sonora Station totals 3,300 acres, located about 27 miles south of Sonora, Texas. Research at Sonora Station has covered all facets of rangelands, including small ruminant management and production, grazing systems, water management, prescribed fire and grazing with goats to reduce juniper invasion for savanna restoration, wildlife ecology, and rangeland plant ecology to name a few. Datasets from some of these projects span decades to inform and support future work. In addition to Sonora Station, the San Angelo Center also manages two other Texas A&M AgriLife Research ranches where similar research is conducted. Read Ranch (Crockett County) totals about 5,000 acres located near Ozona, Texas and the Carl and Bina Sue Martin Ranch totals about 4,700 acres located near Menard, Texas.

The successful candidate will have opportunities to conduct research across the properties associated with the center and collaborate extensively across Texas A&M AgriLife, other universities, governmental agencies, industry partners, and nonprofit organizations to develop impactful research programs that address regional, national, and global challenges in rangeland management and precision livestock systems. These activities will support the missions and strategic plans of the San Angelo Research and Extension Center and Texas A&M AgriLife Research.

Description
Ongoing monitoring of free-roaming cheetahs within a 27,000-hectare (66,700-acre) nature reserve in Limpopo, South Africa, provides a basis for investigating their movements and population ecology. By combining photographic records and spatial information, the project contributes to our understanding of how individual cheetahs use the landscape and how their movements and activity patterns change over time.

Research Focus:
Monitoring cheetahs through camera trap surveys
Identifying individual animals from distinctive coat patterns
Maintaining and expanding photographic identification records
Recording locations and movements to investigate spatial use of the reserve
Examining patterns in habitat use, activity, and distribution
Processing and interpreting data collected through ongoing monitoring

Working with a long-term dataset allows interns to contribute to an ongoing monitoring programme while developing a practical understanding of cheetah ecology. The information collected can help track individuals over time and provide valuable insight into how cheetahs move through and utilise a dynamic bushveld landscape.

Interns will gain practical experience in wildlife identification, camera trap monitoring, field data collection, spatial ecology, and ecological data analysis. The project combines fieldwork with data management and interpretation, providing valuable experience in applied carnivore research and conservation.

Ideal Candidates:
Students or recent graduates with a background in biology, ecology, zoology, wildlife management, or a related discipline
A strong interest in carnivore ecology and wildlife conservation

The minimum duration is 2 months.

SUMMARY:

The Arkansas Game and Fish Commission (AGFC) Conservation Program Biologist II (FISHERIES DIVISION) is responsible for supervising a fisheries management resource. This position is governed by state and federal laws and agency/institution policy.

Supervises a small to medium-sized professional staff by interviewing, recommending hire or termination, assigning and reviewing work, evaluating employee performance, and training employees
Addresses program, district, hatchery, and divisional administrative duties
Directs the planning, preparation, and implementation of projects on Arkansas’ streams, rivers, reservoirs, and fish culture facilities.
Develops aquatic species conservation plans, aquatic species management plans, stream and river management plans, and reservoir management plans.
Coordinates and leads biological surveys and studies of aquatic fauna, determining vital rate functions that shape population structure and condition. 
Statistically analyzes data, writes summary reports, and publishes peer-reviewed journal articles.
Coordinates the gathering of public input through public meetings, angler creel surveys, and other survey methods.
Communicates regularly with the appropriate assistant chief and/or fisheries district coordinators regarding oversight for budgets, contracts, and grants.

Must maintain close individual contact with and develop solid working relationships with all Fisheries Division, agency, and partner organization personnel

SPECIFIC JOB DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES:

As an AGFC District Fisheries Supervisor (Conservation Program Biologist II), you will join a highly trained, progressive team of fisheries scientists working to improve conservation and management of aquatic resources in Arkansas. You will receive outstanding training and competitive pay and benefits, and will be responsible for fisheries management activities within a district, with opportunities to collaborate on projects throughout the state.

Job duties include:

•Standardized fish population surveys
•Onsite and offsite angler surveys
•Stakeholder engagement
•Fish habitat improvement projects and analysis of survey data
•Preparation of annual fishery sample report management plans
•All district administrative duties
•Fishing access development

This position is located in southwest Arkansas and spans the southern Ouachita Mountains and western South Central Plains ecoregions. Fisheries resources are abundant and include: the Red, Cossatot, Little Missouri, and Saline rivers, as well as lakes Millwood, Dierks, DeQueen, Gillham, Bois D'Arc, and Mercer Bayou. This position works under the supervision of the Fisheries District Coordinator in the Management Section of the Fisheries Division

•Knowledge of fisheries principles and techniques
•Knowledge of laboratory and field survey equipment, techniques, and procedures
•Knowledge of supervisory practices and procedures

•Ability to plan work unit objectives and operational activities and to assign and direct the work of subordinates

•Good written and verbal communication skills
•Physically able to work long hours, sometimes under harsh or physically demanding conditions
•Strong teamwork skills, yet capable of completing a task without close supervision
•Strong organizational skills.

The formal education equivalent of a bachelor's degree in biology, ecology, fisheries management, or a related field; plus three years of experience in fisheries or a related field, including one year in a leadership capacity.

Description

The Holbrook Team and Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW) are recruiting a Research Scientist to join them at the University of Wyoming (work location will be in Laramie, WY). The Research Scientist will primarily be working at the intersection of elk behavioral ecology and human recreation. We have deployed an extensive network of trail counters and cameras, as well as GPS units to recreationists, to sample human recreation. We have also acquired privatized human mobility data to add to our sample of humans recreating on our landscapes of interest.  Additionally, over the last 6 years, our team has deployed GPS collars on 280 adult female elk in the two main study locations. The main objective for this position is to advance our understanding regarding human-elk interactions, and provide guidance on recreation development into the future. Recreation is multi-billion dollar economy, and generating insights that inform the development conversation for wildlife conservation is really our hope with this position. 

See the following webpages for more information on the Holbrook Team (https://sites.google.com/site/josephdholbrook03/) at the University of Wyoming. 

Candidates should have expertise in a suite of modeling approaches aimed at understanding animal-habitat relationships and animal movement. Wildlife Innovations is building a bench of experienced avian biologists we can call on for nesting bird surveys, preconstruction avian surveys, nest and burrow monitoring, and compliance monitoring for sensitive and special-status species across coastal Southern California. Assignments are matched to your availability and to project schedules; there is no minimum hours commitment. 

This is a flexible, project-based role well suited to a biologist who wants variable hours, the ability to pick up assignments around an existing schedule, and potential opportunities for specialized training. Further, biologists who demonstrate exemplary performance may be offered the chance to join the Wildlife Innovations’ full-time team. 


WHAT YOU'LL DO

•    Conduct preconstruction and nesting bird surveys, adhering to the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, California Fish and Game Code, and project-specific permit conditions 

•    Identify Southern California birds by sight and sound, including raptors, corvids, shorebirds, and the special-status species relevant to each site 

•    Locate, flag, age, and/or monitor active nests; establish and enforce mitigation measures (when applicable) and communicate results in real time to project biologists and construction crews

We are a DGS-certified small/micro business specializing in wildlife research, monitoring, and management. We work across active construction sites, airports, military installations, ports, and state and city parks, with most of our staff cross-trained across various projects, including those requiring specialized training and certifications. 

Our work is grounded in understanding the relationships between species in local ecosystems and the stressors created by human modification of the landscape. We use advanced monitoring and surveillance techniques to design strategies that resolve wildlife conflicts, reduce impacts during construction, improve management outcomes, and support the recovery of focal species.

COMPENSATION AND ENGAGEMENT

THE ROLE

The Predator Biologist conducts and/or oversees surveillance, research, and targeted management of high threat predators of special status species, including but not limited to nesting California Least Terns and Western Snowy Plovers, in coastal San Diego, Orange, and/or Los Angeles Counties. This is applied and adaptive conservation work, with the data collected used to help steer management efforts both locally and regionally, with the goal of developing and implementing innovative equipment and techniques to increase program efficiency, reduce negative impacts to native predator populations, and achieve recovery goals. 

Day-to-day operations will be based on predator and prey activity, driven by diurnal and nocturnal physical and digital surveillance of nesting and adjacent areas and post-predation site investigations. Active management of high-threat individuals may include a variety of non-lethal and lethal tactics tailored to the species, behavior, and permit conditions. All activity will be digitally collected and analyzed for technical reporting and further development of the programs. Work may include development and testing of experimental techniques to address special status species conflict and GPS tracking of predator movements. Additionally, some work may require injured and contaminated wildlife recovery and transport, as part of on-call rescue projects or oil spill response.

Serve as the agency’s fishery management lead for the Puyallup Basin and East Kitsap area, guiding research and management efforts for fish populations.

Lead work that turns field data and scientific analysis into practical management strategies that protect native fish and wildlife and support sustainable fisheries. 


What to Expect:
Among the varied range of responsibilities held within this role, the Area Fisheries Biologist will, 

Develop preseason management plans for salmon and steelhead that meet conservation objectives while providing recreational fishing opportunity within Pierce and Kitsap County: 
Independently design, and conduct field studies to monitor annual abundance of salmon and steelhead spawning populations. 
Analyze and communicate results through final written products including peer reviewed and/or agency publications, as well as oral presentations to agency staff, co-managers, and others. 
Design and develop preseason and in-season fishing models that estimate impacts from recreational fisheries . 
Stay current with peer reviewed publications regarding new methodologies for salmon and steelhead management.

Manage the Inland Fish Program (lowland and high lakes, resident and anadromous cutthroat, rainbow trout and bull trout in streams and rivers, as well as warm water species in lowland lakes) within Pierce and East Kitsap Counties:
Develop and conduct studies to evaluate the relative success of various stocking strategies.
Conduct spawning ground surveys for steelhead, bull trout, coastal cutthroat trout and resident rainbow trout by foot, pontoon boat, or aerial surveys in helicopters. 
Assist with warm water surveys to sample warmwater fish assemblages in inland lakes. 

Represent WDFW as a technical expert during the annual North of Falcon (NOF) salmon fisheries planning process with tribal co-managers and NOAA:
Develop preseason forecast models for Pacific salmon species that are used in the annual NOF salmon fisheries planning process. 
Provide annual stock abundance estimates and design and manage hatchery programs to achieve fishery and conservation objectives. 
Implement creel surveys and use catch data to model impacts from recreational fisheries on salmon and steelhead populations. 
Provide technical support for the District Biologist and Regional Program Manager in policy discussions.

Monitor and assist in Fish Passage Programs in the Puyallup Watershed:
Collaborate with Tribal Co-managers and Federal Agencies in both the Electron Hydro Project on the Puyallup River and the Mud Mountain Dam Fish Passage Facility on the White River to collect biological samples, assess fish passage, assist with fish rescue events, and provide technical assistance. 
Serve as a member of the South Sound Spring Chinook Technical Committee (SSSCTC) and provide technical expertise. 


Working Conditions:

Work setting, including hazards:
Much of the field work is conducted in remote locations, on unstable terrain or in and around moving water. 
Field work may involve risks such as trips and falls, water-related hazards operating a vehicle, motorboat, raft, and pontoon boat as well as conducting aerial surveys in helicopters. Other hazards may include extreme temperatures, stinging insects and plants, and wildlife encounters.
Survey long distances independently and often for long hours. 
This position may involve working in or near water, including tasks that require navigating, negotiating, and performing duties related to water environments.

Schedule: Typically, Monday – Friday, 8:00 AM – 5:00 PM, 40 hours per week. Flexible work schedule is needed and may include weekends depending on the time of year and longer than 8 hours per day. A 50:50 position split between an office working environment in-person at the Natural Resources Building and scheduled field work.

Travel Requirements: Travel and overnight stays are infrequent but required occasionally.

Strong analytical skills and experience with statistical methods and modeling options for fisheries, population estimates, and the development of escapement goals and recovery plans.

Position Description
Funding is available for up to two years for a postdoctoral research position to work with Drs. Robert Lonsinger and Sue Fairbanks in the Department of Natural Resource Ecology and Management (NREM) at Oklahoma State University.
 This position is funded by the Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation (ODWC) and will be tasked with combining data sources to evaluate population trajectories using multiple competing approaches including standard matrix population models, stochastic projection models, and integrated population models (IPMs). The selected applicant will lead work that expands on our previous research quantifying demography and movement of a recovering population of black bears in southeastern Oklahoma (the Ouachita population). The postdoctoral fellow will (1) collate data from previous research and monitoring efforts, (2) evaluate potential efficacy of monitoring strategies, (3) assess the influence of alternative harvest scenarios identified in concert with ODWC biologists on population dynamics, and (4) work closely with ODWC biologists to identify alternative population management objectives and estimate Prescribed Take Limits to achieve those alternatives. The postdoctoral fellow will be expected to (5) contribute to monthly and annual reporting requirements for the project, and (6) disseminate results via professional presentations and peer-reviewed papers. The selected candidate may also have opportunities to contribute to undergraduate teaching within NREM.
 Well-qualified individuals with a strong quantitative modeling background, experience working with large data sets, experience with IPMs, and research interests in population ecology and harvest management of game species are encouraged to apply. Experience working with state agencies is also beneficial. In addition to collaborating with Drs. Lonsinger and Fairbanks, the postdoctoral fellow will collaborate closely with an interdisciplinary research team that includes Dr. Omkar Joshi (OSU), Dr. Dana Morin (Mississippi State University), and two graduate students funded on the same project.

Salary for this postdoctoral fellow position is $67,000/yr plus benefits excluding retirement. Check out our competitive benefits and eligibility at https://hr.okstate.edu/prospective-ee.html.

Applicants must have earned a Ph.D. in ecology, conservation biology, natural resource management, or a related field before the start date; demonstrated experience conducting research that results in peer-reviewed publications; strong quantitative analysis skills including experience managing and analyzing large data sets or building IPMs; strong written and oral communications skills; and a strong record of successfully leading and participating in collaborative team research.

Job Description:
The Center for Wildlife Sustainability Research at Southern Illinois University is seeking multiple Deer Research Technicians and Lead Technicians to assist with white-tailed deer research across Illinois. This project is conducted in collaboration with the Illinois Department of Natural Resources and focuses on white-tailed deer movement, disease ecology, and population density estimation.

These positions provide extensive hands-on experience with wildlife capture and handling, GPS telemetry, biological sampling, camera trapping, and multiple approaches to estimating deer abundance. Technicians will serve as the primary field staff for the project and work closely with SIU graduate students, project staff, partnering agencies, landowners, and volunteers.

Primary responsibilities include:

Capture and collaring of deer via clover traps, drop nets, and dart guns
Handling and processing captured deer, including:
GPS collar fitting
Disease sampling
Blood drawls
Nasal and oral swabs
Ear tag and ear biopsy
Morphometric measurements
Age and body condition assessments
Conducting nighttime deer density road surveys using vehicle-mounted forward-looking infrared (FLIR) cameras
Deploying and retrieving large-scale camera grids
Scouting, baiting, and preparing deer capture sites
Checking trap lines and monitoring drop-net and darting sites
Mortality investigations
Processing biological samples in the lab, including centrifuging blood, pipetting plasma and serum.
Entering, organizing, and conducting QA/QC of field data
Maintaining and repairing traps, capture equipment, cameras, and other field gear
Maintaining professional relationships with private landowners, volunteers, and partnering agencies
 Timeline:
We anticipate hiring six positions beginning November 18, 2026 (four technicians and two lead technicians) and two additional technician positions beginning January 4, 2027. Preference for the November positions will be given to applicants who can work the full field season. The January positions will begin with deer capture operations and are expected to continue through the spring FLIR survey and camera retrieval period.

Applicants who are available for the capture period but cannot remain through the spring survey period may still be considered, particularly if they have substantial relevant experience with large-mammal capture and handling. Please clearly indicate your preferred start date and availability in the body of your application email.

November 18 – December 22, 2026: Deer density surveys and camera deployment
Technicians will be divided between two crews operating in northwestern and northeastern Illinois. Work will primarily consist of nighttime FLIR road surveys, deployment of camera grids, and associated field work. This portion of the position will involve substantial driving and hiking. Technicians should expect to work through Thanksgiving.

December 23, 2026 – January 3, 2027: Holiday break
All crews will receive a scheduled 12-day break over the Christmas and New Year period.

January 4 – March 31, 2027: Deer capture season
Technicians will transition to two capture crews operating in central and southern Illinois. This will be the capture-intensive portion of the position and will include clover trapping, drop-netting, remote darting, deer handling and processing, biological sampling, GPS collar deployment, and associated field and laboratory work.

April 1 – April 24, 2027: Deer density surveys and camera retrieval
Crews will conduct a second round of FLIR surveys and retrieve camera grids following the capture season.

The exact end date is somewhat flexible and will depend on capture progress, survey schedules, and individual technician hours. Positions are expected to conclude between mid-March and late April 2027, or when the maximum appointment limit of 900 hours is reached.

Location:
Multiple sites in Illinois.

Salary:
Base pay starting at $16.00/hour but commensurate with experience. Lead technicians start at $18/hour. 

Housing is provided throughout the duration of the position.

Qualifications:

Required Qualifications: 
 Applicants should have academic training in wildlife or related field. Must be willing to work long hours in the field, performing physically strenuous tasks outdoors in adverse weather conditions, including extreme cold at times (trapping equipment weighing >50lbs needs to be moved regularly, and adult deer must be physically restrained before anesthesia is administered). Must have prior experience in off-road driving 4-wheel drive vehicles. Required qualifications also include an enthusiasm for outdoor work with wildlife, getting along with your crewmates, reading maps and navigating independently (sometimes without cellular service), demonstrate organizational and communication skills, attention to detail, ability to follow study protocols, and carefully record data. Driver’s license required.
 
 Preferred Qualifications: 
 Highly qualified applicants will have prior experience in large mammal and/or adult deer captures, radio telemetry, chemical immobilization, mortality investigations, and camera trapping.

Lead technician applicants should meet most preferred qualifications, plus have experience in a leadership role and have exceptional communication skills for interactions with the public, partnering agencies, and with SIU staff. Must be able to create a work schedule and delegate tasks.

Please email a cover letter, CV, and three references combined into a single PDF to Tadao Kishimoto at [email removed].

We are hiring one (1) seasonal Wildlife Technician to assist with a project surveying for plains spotted skunks and other mesocarnivores in southeastern Oklahoma from ~January 12 through ~May 7, 2027. Spotted skunks are rare and elusive mesocarnivores that were recently petitioned to be listed under the Endangered Species Act. This study continues and expands upon research on plains spotted skunk population ecology and landcover associations conducted since 2023 (See Brosend et al. 2026 in Wildlife Biology).  The selected candidate will work closely with a graduate student to conduct camera surveys and live trapping for plains spotted skunks and possible side projects related to the study. The selected candidate must be able and willing to hike long distances (up to 20 km per day), over difficult terrain, in potentially extreme conditions (e.g., both cold winter conditions and warm spring temperatures and humidity). The use of olfactory lures is a daily occurrence and those with sensitivities to unsavory smells should consider this when applying. Additionally, candidates with a current rabies vaccine, live-capture experience and previous animal handling experience are encouraged to apply, though these skills are not necessary and those without will not be penalized during the selection process. Attention to detail, a good attitude, and a good work ethic are essential for this position! The selected candidate should anticipate, and be comfortable with, having limited connectivity (i.e., internet or cellular service) and shared (potentially co-ed) living conditions in a small cabin (or similar accommodations).

• Progress towards a bachelor’s degree in wildlife ecology, biology, ecology, or closely related field

• Ability to lift and carry over 50 pounds

• Demonstrated ability to effectively communicate with coworkers and supervisors

• Ability to maintain a positive and mature attitude and good sense of humor, even under harsh, inclement, or uncomfortable conditions (e.g., inclement weather, biting insects, venomous snakes)

• ≥6 months of field experience with wildlife surveys, demonstrating an ability to work in a remote setting and hike over difficult terrain

• Highly motivated with a strong work ethic

• A valid US driver’s license (without restrictions)

Desired Qualifications:

• B.S. in wildlife management, natural resources, or a closely related discipline

• Experience using camera traps to monitor wildlife as part of an ecological study

• Experience running trap lines with box traps

• Experience driving pickup trucks with and without a trailer attached, and/or in 4WD

                             1321 Salazar Rd, Taos, New Mexico 87571

Schedule: The position follows a seasonal schedule that varies based on program operations and needs.
Spring: Primarily spike schedule (Tuesday - Tuesday, eight 10 hour days) with additional office days as needed

Winter: Monday–Friday

Supervision Exercised: Exercises supervision over Crew Supervisors and Field Technicians. Provides substantial indirect supervision of Assistant Crew Leads & Crew Members
Supervision Received: Receives general supervision from the Upper Rio Grande Program Manager; indirect supervision by Conservation Program Director and Executive Director 

Position Summary: The Conservation Program Coordinator serves as a central point of coordination for program execution, connecting RMYC program staff, Crew Supervisors, Corpsmembers, and project partners to ensure that crews are prepared, supported, and operating safely and effectively throughout every aspect of the program year. The Coordinator serves as a primary point of contact and resource for Crew Supervisors and Members, providing guidance, problem-solving, training, and coordination across the full range of program needs. The Conservation Program Coordinator is responsible for ensuring that planning and technical needs are fully addressed, drawing on broad conservation knowledge and problem-solving skills. The Coordinator provides field-based technical leadership, trains crews in conservation practices, monitors project quality and progress, adapts plans to address changing conditions and challenges, and serves as a key resource for risk management and incident response. The Coordinator plays a meaningful role in shaping the culture, standards, and direction of the conservation program. The role requires a strong and steady leadership presence, someone who is engaged and approachable, remains calm and effective when challenges arise, and provides clear direction. The Coordinator must be technically credible and thoughtful in their decision-making, with the adaptability and interpersonal skills to lead in the field, and foster a supportive and accountable team culture. 

Major Responsibilities
Program & Project Operations
Coordinate the successful delivery of conservation projects based out of RMYC’s Upper Rio Grande office from project setup through completion, ensuring projects are effectively planned, resourced, staffed, implemented, and completed to RMYC and partner expectations.
Serve as a central point of coordination among RMYC program staff, Crew Supervisors, Corpsmembers, and project partners throughout project preparation, implementation, and closeout.
Translate project plans into effective field implementation in close coordination with the Project Manager.
Monitor project progress and crew needs continuously, responding to emerging challenges and providing hands-on operational support throughout the season.


Orientation & Training
Design and deliver seasonal orientation intensive that prepares staff and Corpsmembers to safely and effectively carry out their roles and conservation projects.
Develop and adapt training curriculum based on program requirements and crew-specific needs, incorporating technical conservation skills, crew leadership and management, safety and risk management, youth development, and program practices.
Coordinate and facilitate training delivery, including instructors, locations, schedules, curriculum, logistics, and hands-on instruction.
Provide ongoing field training and technical support throughout project delivery, adapting instruction as crews encounter unfamiliar practices, equipment, or site conditions.

Safety, Risk Management & Incident Response
Integrate safety and risk management into program planning, decision-making, training, and field operations.
Serve as the primary program resource for assessing and managing risk associated with field operations 
Respond to incidents and emerging safety concerns, coordinating appropriate support and intervention as needed.

Field Operations
Provide hands-on field leadership and operational support to ensure crews have the resources, coverage, and logistical support needed to succeed.
Provide temporary or extended field coverage when staffing needs require, including assuming Crew Supervisor responsibilities at project locations across New Mexico for periods ranging from individual days to multiple weeks.
Support project logistics and field coordination across project locations in New Mexico.

Crew Personnel Coordination
Lead the recruitment, hiring, onboarding, and personnel processes for Crew Supervisors, Assistant Crew Leaders, and Corpsmembers.
Manage ongoing personnel and administrative processes throughout the season, ensuring required documentation, records, changes, and other personnel requirements are completed accurately, consistently, and on time.

Corpsmember Support & Development
Provide ongoing support and guidance to Corpsmembers, serving as a trusted point of contact for wellness, development, sometimes in challenging or sensitive situations.
Respond to Corpsmember needs throughout the season, helping participants navigate personal, interpersonal, and program-related challenges.
Provide timely support and intervention when urgent or emerging needs arise, including situations requiring immediate travel or response outside of regular working hours.

Other Responsibilities
Support Project Manager in partner outreach and project generation and planning
